0.title: Assignment 1: Create a dataset
0.content: Due: 9 am, Fri Oct 16 → Submit to Canvas. Mimi Onuoha’s art project “The Library of Missing Datasets” illuminates what we value and what we ignore in an increasingly data-saturated world. For example, there is little data that exists about financial transactions in the art market (especially between gallerists and artists) and on US judges and case outcomes. Think of a dataset that doesn’t exist and create it. This could be as grandiose or as mundane as you would like: it could be the temperature of a patch of grass outside your room for a week, FitBit or other health tracking data, or more substantial research on social or political phenomena. (For example, the Data Against Feminicide project required scores of volunteers to track feminicide throughout Latin American by reading through innumerable news articles to collect data that governments did not.) There is no requirement around time span or number of observations in this dataset; the “Dogs of Cambridge” dataset is not bounded by time the way that temperature is. This dataset does need to demonstrate clear inclusion and exclusion criteria, require some kind of measurement apparatus, and provide you with enough information to do some analysis about what the data shows. To complete the assignment, you will submit the dataset, a write-up about the data collection process / what the data shows, and a data visualization of your choice.

Write one sentence per reading justifying its position relative to the others. In one sentence, identify one adjacent-ranking pair that you might expect me to ask about and preview your reasoning. | . This is an open-book, analog exam: you can bring hard copies of your class notes, readings, previous assignments, etc. and refer to them at any time.

16.title: Late work
16.content: There are no grading penalties for late work, but late work gets no written comments. Turning something in late means you miss the window in which I have time set aside to read it carefully. You are always welcome to come to office hours and we can talk about the assignment instead. This flexibility easily applies to A1. For A2, you get to pick the exam time of your choice, so this does not really apply. This policy is a little more difficult with A3 as it is built on milestones that help you slowly develop the project throughout the arc of the class. A late submission throws off everything after it (e.g., you submit a first draft late → your colleagues give you comments late → you can’t implement changes in time for the presentation). These dependencies make it difficult to veer away from the schedule. The two oral components (the peer review draft and the final presentation) happen in class on assigned dates and cannot be moved. The only date that is flexible in any way is the submission of the final paper, which is due on December 4. The latest you can turn in the final paper is December 15, which is the day that grades are due. Alas, these are Institute rules and I cannot bend them.

17.title: Completion-based assignments
17.content: These assignments are graded by completion: we’re interested in process, not perfection.

18.title: Reading responses
18.content: For each of set of readings, you will have an opportunity to write a ~3-5 sentence response to a given prompt. (This may be during class or at the end of class.) The prompts may include the following formats: . | Define a keyword: explain how it might apply to an example not in the reading. | Method autopsy: what did the author actually do to arrive at their conclusion? What is the data? The unit? Analytical method? | Three-sentence summary: what question was the author trying to answer? How did they do it? What is the argument? | Quote interpretation: here is a selected quote from the reading; write 3-5 sentences about why it matters or how it works in the rest of the reading | Agree / disagree: I will put up a statement about the reading; write whether the author would agree or disagree with the statement. | TIL: what did you learn today? Why is it important, significant, interesting…? | Charitable disagreement: what is the strongest argument against the reading and how might the author respond? | . The responses are primarily graded for completion and engagement, not correctness: ✔️+ (1.5 points), ✔️ (1 pt), ✔️ - (0.5 pt). Your total for this component is capped at 19 points, so a ✔️+ can offset a ✔️ - or a session you miss.

19.title: Attendance
19.content: You must speak at least once in class per session in order to receive attendance and participation points (one per class). There are no make-up assignments or excused absences for this, as there are over 100 points available in this grading schema. For one-off absences because of illness or other conflicts, not being able to make up these lost attendance points is very unlikely to make a difference in your final grade.

21.title: Acknowledgements
21.content: Like many other prestigious institutions of higher education, MIT was founded by a slave owner and materially benefited from the sale of enslaved people. MIT’s third president rose to fame as the leader of the Bureau of Indian Affairs, whose task was to forcibly remove Indigenous people. The Institute also played an important role in building the military-industrial-academic complex during WWII. In 2019, the New Yorker uncovered the MIT Media Lab’s donations from Jeffrey Epstein, whose wealth has been indelibly tied to sex trafficking. The point in acknowledging these realities is not to guilt or shame anyone, but to recognize how the many privileges we enjoy at MIT — world-class research facilities, fancy speakers — are funded by efforts that involve enormous exploitation. What does this mean for the work we do here? MIT’s official motto suggests that we must acquire knowledge and apply it in a way that benefits the world: we should do so while being mindful of these histories, lest we further contribute to these problems. This class is intended to help untangle the many social complexities at the intersection of technology and society so that we can all construct a more just future. These class policies, readings, and exercises rely heavily on resources from Blakeley H. Payne, Casey Fiesler, Justin Reich, Shannon Mattern, Jonathan Sterne, Ed Bertschinger, T.L. Taylor, Ashley Shew, Damien Patrick Williams, Lydia XZ Brown, Yoel Roth, Jeremy Weinstein, Mehran Sahami, Rob Reich, Kendra Albert, and many others. In some cases, I have shamelessly copied directly from their fantastic syllabi. Assignment 1 was adapted from an assignment created by Jonathan Zong and Janet Zong York in their course “AI, Justice, Imagination: Technology and Speculative Fiction.” . The class draws heavily on materials and examples found online, and I try my best to give credit by linking to the original source. Please contact me (crystall at mit dot edu) if you find materials where credit is missing, or that you would rather have removed.

38.title: Community guidelines
38.content: An important part of our initial class conversation is co-creating a set of community guidelines. Here are some important starting components that will hold for the rest of this course. | Don’t be an asshole. This is far and away the most important rule in our class. It is your job to treat everyone in our class with care so that we can all learn together. Please expect to be both challenged and valued. As such, I will not tolerate harassment in the classroom. A corollary: an important part of not being an asshole is making a good faith effort to do the work. We will never have the correct answer when it comes to these complicated issues, but it is important to make a good faith effort to try and understand the stakes of the problem. | No bullshit. Intellectual community is a precious resource, so we should make the most of it. In class, we will always respond to the best possible version of an opposing argument, and do so after carefully engaging with the reading (and each other). While I’ve tried to make “bangers only” a guiding policy in choosing readings, there is no getting around the fact that there is a lot of reading in this class. Please don’t fake your way through class, particularly through the summarization feature in a chatbot; being in class with that person sucks. If you find yourself often taking up a lot of space in class, please encourage others to step up and highlight ideas from people who have not been getting the same air time. A corollary: no devil’s advocates. | Create a space for open learning and trust. One goal of the class is to allow us to critically and productively examine issues around media, science, and technology that are often sensitive, controversial, and challenging. This means that while there will be materials from the course available for access purposes, I will not record our sessions — to protect both student privacy and the intellectual honesty and openness of our shared discussions. If you have any questions as to what or whether to share something publicly from the class, particularly on social media, please practice active and enthusiastic consent and reach out to the speaker you are quoting for explicit approval. In this class we use the Chatham House Rule when it comes to sharing specifics from our conversations, so please do not tag others publicly without their consent. That being said, please feel free to widely share the course materials — syllabi, recommended materials, readings — from this class, and to adapt them for your own purposes (workshops, IAP courses, and so on). I only ask that you practice responsible citation practices. I would love to know how this class has a life outside of our time together, and I love seeing students succeed. | It’s okay not to agree with one another. This also means that you do not have to agree with me, the assigned readings, or even the majority of your classmates to do well in the course. You are, however, obligated to demonstrate an understanding of the course material regardless of whether or not you agree with it. | . We will discuss and create additional guidelines together in the first week. Those collaboratively designed guidelines will be added here and will apply to all of our discussions.

39.title: Approach to generative AI
39.content: There are two tracks available in this class. You can use AI as a support tool, or you can be a conscientious objector and avoid it completely. You choose your track in the second class, and it is entirely possible to do this class without AI, with no adaptations. | The AI declaration | Official MIT policy | My general approach | Promises I will make to you | .

40.title: The AI declaration
40.content: Fri Sep 11: In your AI declaration, tell me which track you are choosing and how you would be interested in using AI, if applicable. From there, we will craft a generative AI policy together for those who choose to use it. “Use Claude for editing and research support” is so squishy that it is actually quite difficult to have a shared understanding of what it means, so we will do the work of pinning it down as a class. For conscientious objectors: it is possible to do the class entirely without AI, with no adaptations.

41.title: Official MIT policy
41.content: This subject follows MIT’s B2 policy (Limited GenAI use): students may use generative AI to support learning, brainstorming, editing, debugging, or generating explanations, but may not use it to produce full or substantial assignment solutions. Assignments will clearly specify the stages or components that allow and disallow use, and “assistance” or “support” will be defined for each assignment.

42.title: My general approach
42.content: I will defend to the death the value of being able to think, read, and write without the help of a computer. I don’t think generative AI is the same as using a calculator. Even so, knowing multiplication tables — a form of rote memorization! — is still something we do because it helps us do more advanced thinking more quickly. We’re trying to do something more or less the same: to exercise the muscles that help us read and write.

43.title: Promises I will make to you
43.content: . | I will disclose my own AI use in class. For example, for this syllabus, I used Claude to list out all of the dates for the semester, help me plan when milestones should be due around the holidays, and look up best practices on assignment and assessment design (I asked Claude to collect PDF guides published by university teaching centers). After writing out everything without AI assistance into a LibreOffice document, I asked Claude Code to update the files in this course website repository. | I will never feed any of your writing into any generative AI system. Similarly, I will never put your writing through any “AI detection” software, nor will I ask you to download any spyware in order to create an “AI-free” writing environment. | I will never use generative AI to generate comments on your work. Everything you write will be read and commented on 100% without AI. No summarization, no “check this essay for major weaknesses.” . | Your skill at using generative AI will not be evaluated in this class. Nor will it necessarily give you an advantage. It is entirely possible to do this entire class without AI and for it to be equally (if not more) rewarding. | .

45.title: How this class works
45.content: This class will largely be run in an analog fashion: no electronics in class unless required for an activity. Most activities are done on pen and paper. We will write in carbonless notebooks for reading responses and first drafts—partly because I don’t want you to have to download and use spyware, and mostly because I want you to be able to think and write for yourself without a computer. I also want to acknowledge that moving all writing into the classroom is not a productive exercise. Timed writing often tests knowledge under pressure, not quality of thought. So the in-class writing here is for invention, not assessment: it is graded for effort and engagement, not correctness or fluency. You will bring all readings to class in hard copy. You will be able to consult them during reading responses, discussion, and other in-class work.

46.title: Reading and reading responses
46.content: There will be both in-class and at-home reading. I will bring copies of the in-class readings. Reading check-ins are low-stakes, quick writing exercises to seed conversation and make sure everyone is on the same page with the required reading. You could interpret them as “gotchas” to make sure you did the reading; they are primarily intended to give you practice interpreting and engaging with a text in written form. They are graded for completion, clarity, and effort. How to succeed at reading check-ins . | Bring hard copies of the readings and your notes. These will be in both open- and closed-book format, and there will be no advance notice as to which. | Be ready to interpret, synthesize, and share. This is not about perfect writing. It is about exercising your skills of interpretation and analysis. | . You will receive written feedback on these responses. They are your chance to engage with the take-home readings, and I will receive a copy from your notebook. Keep the original because you will bring it to the midterm oral exam and may refer to it in other contexts.

47.title: Scaffolded writing
47.content: You will have in-class time to begin your larger writing assignments. The exercises are scaffolded so that we can keep track of your progress as the assignment develops. For Assignment 1, for example, I have allocated time for us to write protocol pre-registrations; these drafts are turned in at the end of class but are not graded for completion or correctness. These serve as a benchmark for how your writing is developing, and give you space to think in a purely analog fashion. I will review that draft — without grading it, though feedback is available on request — and take it into account when reviewing the final assignment.

51.title: Attendance and general wellbeing
51.content: If you are ill, exhausted, grieving, or otherwise unwell, go home. Please do not come to class especially if you are ill. You do not need permission, nor to provide any excuse or proof, for missing classes or requesting delays in work due to illness or other personal needs. I appreciate advance notice just so that I can prepare accordingly for class; please be forthright with me so that we can work together to set you up for success. You do not need to share further with me, but I am here to listen if it would be helpful. I will try to provide hybrid access for our class sessions, but I will not record them so that we can keep an open conversation and maintain student privacy. This class is fundamentally designed to be in-person; it will be difficult to succeed in the class if you attend primarily remotely. While I will do my best to ensure that everyone is visible and audible, I also ask that you recognize the difficulty of simultaneously managing physical and virtual environments. There are no make-up assignments for absences. Please review the class materials posted on this site, confer with your classmates, and come to the next class prepared. Note that attendance and participation is only 25 of 160 available points, and reading responses are capped in a way that absorbs a missed session — a one-off absence is very unlikely to change your final grade.

52.title: Grading and late policy
52.content: I take the work you and your colleagues produce very seriously, and I will read it and give thorough, constructive feedback to help sharpen your analysis and communication skills. To that end, I set aside significant blocks of time to make these comments; turning in late work means that you miss the window of opportunity to get feedback. There are no grading penalties for late work, but late work = no comments. Instead, you are free to come to my office hours and we can talk about the assignment in lieu of written comments. Since I ask for all written assignments to be submitted in an editable form (that is, not a PDF), I will make in-line comments that you should feel free to respond to. If you do, please email me so I know to look — I have too many Google Doc notifications to keep track of, and this flag helps. This flexibility applies to the first two assignments. The final project is structured with milestones that build upon each other, which means that if you turn in something late, it throws off the entire schedule. There are oral presentations for both the first draft (for peer feedback) and the final project; those due dates are not movable. You must complete all of the components of the final project in order to successfully complete the class. While I will do everything in my power to be flexible with deadlines (life happens), I do not have the power to bend Institute policies when it comes to grading. The hard deadline for grading this semester is December 15. I need time to grade the papers, so that is the latest you can possibly turn in the final paper. This is particularly important for other Institute guidelines, like deadlines regarding graduation.

53.title: Access needs
53.content: You do not need any kind of medical documentation to seek accommodations in this class. Perhaps you work better with auditory rather than visual materials; we can discuss that. Please come talk to me — in person, via email, via Zoom appointment — and we will figure out what works best for you and for your colleagues. My job is to make the classroom a hospitable working and learning environment for all of my students; please be forthright and clear with me at the beginning of class so that we can maneuver nimbly. While I am happy to work with you on accommodations recognizing all the challenges that you might face inside and outside the classroom, please also respect my time and significant responsibilities, including to your fellow students. If you are unsure of what kinds of accommodation are available to you, the Job Accommodation Network and MIT’s Disability and Access Services have a great set of resources. If you need additional accommodations, or would prefer not to speak to me about it, you may consult Student Support Services (S3) or seek accommodation through Disability and Access Services.

54.title: Incompletes
54.content: The flexible grading system is structured so that you should have ample opportunity to find alternative assignments should you be unable to complete one for any reason. I will grant time-delimited extensions for final assignments; incompletes should not be used as a salve for perfectionism.

55.title: Social media and recording policy
55.content: As noted in the community guidelines, please do not record your colleagues, me, or this class. This class is intended as a forum for folks to learn without fear of being recorded — we’re all going to be working through first-draft thoughts here — and the learning process requires you to be a bit vulnerable. You are free to post about the things you learned in class provided that you respect the privacy of your colleagues and receive explicit and enthusiastic consent. If you have doubts as to what is appropriate, do not hesitate to reach out and ask.

56.title: Academic integrity and plagiarism
56.content: As Kishonna Gray and Sarah Ahmed write, citations determine whose work gets visibility and validation. Science is filled with examples of folks taking credit where none was warranted; in this class, we will not participate in this tradition. Here are MIT’s policies on academic misconduct. Occasionally, you may feel overwhelmed by the amount of work you need to accomplish and may be tempted to cut corners, risking violations of academic integrity that could compromise your academic career. Use these resources instead — they can help you manage your workload and succeed.

57.title: Mandatory reporting
57.content: All instructors (including TAs) at MIT are mandatory reporters. This means that we are obligated to notify the Title IX office if we are given knowledge about sexual assault or violence by other employees and students. Here is a list of confidential resources at MIT; please be advised of the difference between confidential vs. private resources.

58.title: Caregiving and basic needs
58.content: If you have disruptions in childcare, you may bring your child to class as needed. If you need to feed your baby in the classroom, please do so; you may also find this map of campus lactation rooms helpful. If you face difficulty accessing food or lack a safe and stable place to live, please contact MIT Doing Well or VPR Advocacy Services. I have personally found VPR in particular to be tremendously helpful as a resource to talk through different options regarding emotional support, navigating campus procedures, housing relocation, and so on — particularly when you have experienced harm. They can also help you figure out how to support someone you know when they are going through a difficult time.

59.title: Resources
59.content: Places to get help with reading, writing, research, and more.

60.title: Introduction to Media Studies
60.content: CMS.100 – Fall 2026 – Wednesdays and Fridays, 1–2:30 pm (35-308) . This course offers an overview of the social, cultural, political, and economic impact of mediated communication on modern culture. Media covered include the printed word, film, the internet, and digital technologies. All course materials live here. Please check this site regularly: slides are posted here and the readings are subject to change. You will never get more reading than is listed on the calendar; readings may be swapped for something of equivalent length or less. Always refer to this site (not a paper copy!) for the most up-to-date readings and guidelines.

61.title: Learning objectives
61.content: After successfully completing the course, you will be able to: . | Describe the role of media (analog, digital, and otherwise) in persuading, informing, entertaining, and socializing individuals and groups | Explain how we use and make meaning with media as part of everyday experience | Analyze the structure of media institutions / industries and differing systems of organization, funding, and regulation | Evaluate the implications of technological change and the interactions between humans and technologies | . You will also apply these concepts to sharpen your writing and presentation skills, where you will critically analyze and assess the social and political implications of media and technology. Alongside smaller writing assignments, students will also produce a final project that reflects original data collection, research, and analysis. Instructor: Crystal Lee (office hours by appointment) .

64.title: Library and research assistance
64.content: Please apply for a Harvard Library card and use BorrowDirect. The Harvard card gives you access to the physical facilities across campus — studying at the beautiful Law Library, using Harvard buses — and BorrowDirect lets you borrow a book from any library in the network (Princeton, Stanford, Chicago, and more), so there is no need to wait for a book in course reserves when you could just get a copy from another library. If you’re pressed for time, you can request pick-up online, where a lovely librarian will collect all the books you list and you can pick them all up at once at the library of your choosing. If you use Zotero for citation and PDF management — which you should — your MIT email gives you unlimited cloud storage, with all its environmental implications. You should also avail yourself of the book acquisition request form: the libraries will buy virtually any book you suggest through the form that doesn’t already exist in the catalog. I would also highly recommend the extensive research support that the libraries offer. Professor T.L. Taylor has this fantastic guide that is specific to media studies. Several readings on the calendar are hosted behind libproxy.mit.edu. You will need to be signed in with your MIT certificates or through Touchstone to reach them. If a link doesn’t work, try it again from an MIT network or let me know.

65.title: Mental health care
65.content: Being a student at MIT is a very difficult task, and for many, it is the first time that they need assistance with their emotional wellbeing. This can come in many forms: managing social anxiety, being overwhelmed by all of your obligations, feeling foggy and like you’re constantly walking through molasses. Throughout college and grad school, I struggled a great deal (as I still do) with mental health issues. Finding the language to talk about my experience — to say nothing about actually seeking help — was a really long process for me, as I had a lot of internalized stigma about mental health problems. It feels trite to say, but it is no less true: you are not alone. It is okay if all you did today was simply survive. If you are looking for medical care and counseling services at MIT, you can make an appointment here; this scheduling system is not intended for emergency situations. As mentioned in mandatory reporting, MIT Medical, VPR, and ordained clergy are all confidential resources — they cannot disclose to others the contents of your conversations — whereas other entities like S3 are not. If you or a classmate are in a life-threatening situation, you can call, text, or chat the free 24-hour Suicide and Crisis Lifeline at 988. It can be used by anyone, even if you’re feeling sad or hopeless without ideation. If you reach out to 911, please be aware that police are not equipped to offer mental health support and may even pose additional dangers to the person experiencing a crisis. The MA Department of Mental Health also provides these resources. While MIT Medical offers counseling services — which, in my personal experience, has been very positive but requires long lead time — you may seek more specialized health care. MIT Medical itself can give you referrals for providers off campus who will be able to see you more regularly than providers on campus. There is an excellent step-by-step guide from NPR on how to find (and work with) a therapist. Here are some other national directories that you may find helpful: the National Queer and Trans Therapists of Color network, Therapy for Black Girls, Asian-American Therapist Directory, and Therapy for Latinx. If you have suggestions for other services to include (or exclude), please do not hesitate to contact me.

66.title: Office hours
66.content: My office hours — by Zoom and in person in E18-437 — are by appointment. Email me (crystall at mit dot edu) to set one up. Here are some things that we can talk about during my office hours: . | Concepts in the readings, or how the readings and assignments relate to the class | Clarifications on assignments (provided you have clearly read the instructions) | Brainstorming or additional guidance for your writing or other projects | Feedback on your in-class writing, or on fellowship / internship / grad school applications | General input about academic trajectory or careers, keeping in mind that I have spent most of my life in academia with only brief stints outside | Help with navigating MIT resources, to the best of my ability (I learn something new about the Institute all the time) | Feedback on the class, or on particular assignments and materials | Current events and their relationship to the things we study in class | . Above all, I am excited to get to know you—about your plans during and after college, about your interests and activities on campus, and about the things that excite you. One of the joys of being at MIT is having conversations with folks who are really excited by ideas, so please don’t hesitate to have a chat.

67.title: Writing and presentation assistance
67.content: The Writing and Communication Center offers free one-on-one professional advice from communication experts with advanced degrees and publishing experience. If you need assistance on all kinds of academic and professional writing, or want to develop your oral communication skills, make an appointment for a consultation. You can turn to the WCC for class assignment assistance, but they can also help you work on practicing for interviews, fiction and poetry, graduate school applications, conversation practice, technical documentation, note-taking strategies, and help dealing with writing fear. Appointments go fast! .
